first.rationale: The competitor's entry pricing makes promotional_pricing the emotionally obvious move, but the objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, and discount-led acquisition is exactly the lever most likely to buy short-term signups at the cost of revenue quality, margin, and retention. memory_73 is also the single most suspicious item in inherited memory: it is the most confident and most specific claim in the set ('strong acquisition and revenue lift', 'cut time-to-first-value', 'held across both billing plans'), which is the signature of a summary that has accreted certainty across consolidations rather than one grounded in a record that actually tested those things. I want the archived source before acting on it, not after. Second verification goes to memory_86 because onboarding is where the measured decline actually is (completion -4% QoQ, likely feeding activation -6%), and memory_86 plus memory_31 point the same direction from two independent consolidations, which is the strongest converging evidence I have. Intended action is simplify_onboarding: it targets the plausible root cause rather than the competitor's move, it is reversible, and it improves conversion quality of traffic we already have instead of importing price-sensitive churn. Caveat I am holding open: 'shorten onboarding' can degrade downstream value by stripping qualifying fields that route enterprise prospects into self-serve, which memory_44 suggests converts worse on pipeline quality, so the test must be scoped to SMB self-serve and instrumented on qualified-revenue and 30/60-day retention, not just completion rate. Standard experiment scale with those guardrails; if the archive shows memory_86 rests on a thin or completion-only record, I downgrade to a small guarded test rather than switching to pricing.
